title: Redwood demo - Orion Payments (VPC / Private options + audit logging)
summary: Redwood walked Orion Payments through Redwood Console (latency/cost breakdown, traces, rollouts), smart routing + automatic fallback policies, and deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private in a customer VPC/on-prem style topology). Orion asked detailed questions about audit logs (fields, export, retention), regional isolation (single-region, no cross-region failover), and how key management works (KMS/HSM). Redwood aligned on a near-term evaluation: start with a VPC-based pilot for fraud ops + support workflows, define SLOs, and schedule a security review to share the evidence pack under NDA.
topics: Redwood Console overview (dashboards, traces, token cost)
Routing policies and graceful fallback (model variants, region, capacity tiers)
Dedicated vs Private deployments for regulated environments
Audit logs: events, fields, export patterns, retention controls
Regional isolation vs multi-region failover options
Pilot scoping: workload, success criteria, timelines, and owners
next_steps: Redwood (Avery) to send a 1-page deployment options recap (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and recommended architecture for Orion’s VPC constraint.
Redwood (Fatima) to share audit log sample schema + export options and confirm which events are available today vs on roadmap.
Orion (Marcus) to send their security questionnaire and the required audit log / retention requirements list.
Schedule a 45-min security review next week with Orion Security + Redwood Security/GRC (Naomi/Olga as needed).
Set up a pilot kickoff: choose one workload (fraud analyst summarization or support agent assist), define latency and cost targets, and confirm region (us-east-1 preferred).
Orion (Nina) to confirm whether they need strict single-region only (no cross-region DR) or if warm-standby in a second region is acceptable.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: Redwood demo - Orion Payments (VPC / Private options + audit logging)
Date: 2025-05-08
Time: 10:02 AM - 10:54 AM (Pacific)
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference) - AE
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference) - Solutions Engineering
- Fatima Noor (Redwood Inference) - SE, regulated workloads
- Nina Patel (Orion Payments) - Director, Platform Engineering
- Marcus Reed (Orion Payments) - Security Engineer
- Jen Alvarez (Orion Payments) - Fraud Ops Lead
- Tom Kline (Orion Payments) - Procurement

Auto-summary (generated)
- Demo focused on Redwood Console and deployment choices for regulated environments.
- Orion asked about audit logs, data retention, and regional isolation.
- Redwood explained routing/fallback and how it behaves in single-region vs multi-region.
- Next steps include a security review, evidence pack sharing, and pilot scoping.

Action items (as captured)
- Avery: email recap + pilot plan outline by EOD Fri.
- Fatima: audit log schema + example export notes by Mon.
- Orion (Marcus): send security questionnaire + required controls list by Tue.

----

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. I think we’re on. Nina, Marcus, Jen, Tom—thanks for joining. We’ve got Markus and Fatima on from our side. Today’s goal is basically show you the Console, talk through the VPC/private options, and then leave time for the audit logging and region isolation questions you had in email.

[00:21] Nina Patel: Sounds good.

[00:23] Markus Klein: Yep, hi everyone.

[00:25] Fatima Noor: Hey folks.

[00:27] Avery Johnson: Quick agenda: two minutes on what’s in scope, then Markus will do product demo—Console, routing, fallback. Then we’ll do Dedicated versus Private, and we’ll reserve like 15 minutes for Q&A. If we don’t get through all the security stuff, we can do a separate security review.

[00:45] Marcus Reed: We’ll probably want that anyway. But yes, go ahead.

[00:49] Jen Alvarez: I mainly want to see, like, what operators on my team would see. Like dashboards, latency, failure reasons, that sort of thing.

[00:56] Markus Klein: Great, I’ll focus on that.

[01:00] Avery Johnson: Also just a reminder, we’re recording on our side via Fireflies.

[01:05] Nina Patel: OK.

[01:07] Markus Klein: Let me share my screen.

[01:10] (screen share starts)

[01:12] Markus Klein: So this is Redwood Console. I’m in a sandbox org. Left nav is Routes, Models, Deployments, Observability—stuff like that. Most teams start in Routes because it maps to your app endpoints.

[01:28] Jen Alvarez: Routes is like, API endpoints?

[01:30] Markus Klein: Exactly. Like /fraud-summary, /support-assist, or however you want to define. You can bind a route to a model and a policy. The important part is you get per-route latency, token usage, and error breakdown.

[01:46] Markus Klein: If I click Observability… you’ll see a time series for P50/P95 latency, tokens in/out, and then cost. Cost is basically token-based, but we break it down by prompt vs completion so you can see when prompts are ballooning.

[02:03] Jen Alvarez: So for my use case it’s like, some requests are huge because we shove in transaction history.

[02:08] Markus Klein: Exactly. And you can add truncation or summarization upstream, but at least you can see it. We also show streaming vs non-streaming latencies separately because people get confused by that.

[02:21] Nina Patel: Is this pulling from logs or is it like, agent-based?

[02:25] Markus Klein: It’s coming from the request path itself. For hosted it’s obviously in our control plane. For Dedicated and Private, the data path is in your environment; metrics get exported to the Console via a control plane connection you can restrict. We can talk about that more when we hit Private.

[02:44] Marcus Reed: That’s one of the questions. Like, do you need inbound access to our VPC or is it outbound only.

[02:51] Fatima Noor: Typically outbound only, but we’ll cover it in deployment section. We can support very locked down setups.

[02:57] Markus Klein: Staying in Console for a sec—here’s a Trace view. If I click an individual request, you can see the request ID, route, model version, and then breakdown like: queue time, prefill, decode.

[03:11] Jen Alvarez: Prefill and decode… sorry, what’s that?

[03:14] Markus Klein: Prefill is processing the prompt, decode is token generation. In fraud ops you might have long prompts, so prefill dominates; in chatbots decode dominates.

[03:26] Markus Klein: We also surface cache hit rate if prefix caching is enabled. That’s more relevant when you have repeated system prompts or repeated policy text.

[03:38] Nina Patel: You said model version—do we pin a model version? Because we can’t have it change underneath.

[03:43] Markus Klein: Yeah, you can pin a specific version. And then rollouts are explicit. We do canaries, A/B, and you can auto-fallback if error rate or latency crosses threshold.

[03:55] Avery Johnson: And for regulated folks, we’re very careful about “silent upgrades.” So you choose when to update.

[04:02] Marcus Reed: Okay.

[04:04] Markus Klein: Let me jump to Policies. So a policy can be: primary model is, say, Llama-3.1-70B-instruct quantized, fallback is Llama-3.1-8B or maybe a different provider—depending on deployment mode.

[04:19] Nina Patel: Different provider meaning like… OpenAI?

[04:22] Markus Klein: Potentially. But in Private deployments you typically don’t want egress to external APIs. So fallback would be within your cluster or within your allowed region. For hosted, some customers choose multi-provider fallback; for regulated it’s usually “same vendor, same environment” fallback.

[04:41] Marcus Reed: We need “same environment.” Like no external calls.

[04:44] Markus Klein: Got it.

[04:46] Markus Klein: Here’s what fallback looks like. You can do “fallback on capacity,” “fallback on latency,” and “fallback on error types.” For example, if the primary is saturated, route to a smaller model. If the smaller model fails, you can return a graceful error. You can also cap max tokens to protect yourself.

[05:08] Jen Alvarez: Does fallback mean we get inconsistent answers? That’s a big concern.

[05:12] Markus Klein: Yeah, it’s a tradeoff. Most teams set fallback for non-critical routes or they use it to keep the system up with a known lower quality. Some do it only when the system is unhealthy, not as a normal path. And we recommend measuring it with evals.

[05:30] Avery Johnson: The other pattern is: no fallback, but reserve dedicated capacity so you don’t need it. That’s where Dedicated comes in.

[05:37] Nina Patel: Can you talk Dedicated vs Private now? Because we have constraints.

[05:41] Avery Johnson: Yep, let’s do it.

[05:43] Markus Klein: Switching tabs.

[05:46] Markus Klein: So think of three modes: Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (we host it but you get isolated GPU pool), Private (you deploy in your VPC or on-prem). For you, we’re mostly discussing Dedicated or Private because of your data boundary.

[06:03] Nina Patel: Right. We have a rule that anything with customer PII needs to stay in our AWS account. That’s the default.

[06:10] Markus Klein: That points to Private VPC. Dedicated can still meet some customers’ requirements if they allow vendor hosting with isolation and contractual controls, but if policy is “must be in our account,” then Private is usually the answer.

[06:23] Tom Kline: Dedicated is still a contract with you though, right? Like monthly commit.

[06:27] Avery Johnson: Yeah. Dedicated is reserved capacity—monthly or annual commits. Private is more of an enterprise license plus support, and then you run infra costs. We’ll keep it high level today; we can loop in commercial later.

[06:41] Fatima Noor: From a security lens, Private also gives you the strongest controls around network boundaries, key management, logging destinations, and residency—because it’s literally your environment.

[06:53] Marcus Reed: That’s what I need to understand: what logs exist, and where do they go.

[06:58] Markus Klein: Perfect, let’s talk about logs.

[07:00] Markus Klein: In Private, there’s (1) application logs from the inference gateway and runtime, (2) audit logs—events about access and config changes, and (3) metrics/traces.

[07:14] Marcus Reed: Define audit logs. Like who accessed what, when.

[07:18] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Think: user login events (if SSO is enabled), API key creation/rotation, policy changes, route changes, deployment changes, role changes, and administrative actions.

[07:31] Marcus Reed: Do you log prompt content?

[07:33] Fatima Noor: By default we do not recommend logging prompts or completions in audit logs. Audit logs are event metadata, not payload content. For request logging, you can configure sampling and redaction. In regulated deployments, most customers either disable content logging or do strict redaction.

[07:49] Nina Patel: We’d want content off. We can do our own app-level logging if needed.

[07:54] Markus Klein: That’s common.

[07:56] Marcus Reed: What fields are in the audit log event? Like source IP, actor, time, region.

[08:02] Fatima Noor: Typical fields: timestamp, actor (user/service principal), action type, resource type and ID (route ID, policy ID), result (success/failure), and context like IP address and user agent when relevant. For Private, you also know the cluster/namespace because it’s in your environment.

[08:22] Marcus Reed: Export format? We ingest into Splunk.

[08:25] Markus Klein: We can export as JSON lines. Some customers forward via Fluent Bit / Fluentd to Splunk or CloudWatch. If you want a direct Splunk HEC, we’ve seen folks do that too. We can provide an example config.

[08:41] Marcus Reed: Is that available now or is it “roadmap.”

[08:44] Fatima Noor: JSON export is available. The “pretty” turnkey templates vary depending on your environment, but the log stream is there. We’ll follow up with what’s productized vs reference examples.

[08:57] Jen Alvarez: Sorry, in our world “audit log” also means like, every time an agent uses the model, we need a record for compliance.

[09:05] Fatima Noor: Good question. That’s usually “inference request logs” not “admin audit logs.” We support request IDs and metadata. Many customers log request metadata (timestamp, route, model version, token counts, latency, success/failure) without prompt content. That gives you an audit trail without storing PHI/PII.

[09:24] Nina Patel: Can we make request logs mandatory and immutable? Like retention.

[09:28] Markus Klein: Retention is typically handled in your logging backend. We can configure how long the service retains local logs (short), and you forward them to your system for long-term retention.

[09:42] Marcus Reed: We also need to know if logs can cross regions. We have “no cross-region” rules.

[09:48] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk regional isolation specifically.

[09:51] Markus Klein: In Private, if you deploy in us-east-1, everything stays there unless you configure otherwise. There’s no hidden cross-region replication because it’s your AWS account. For Dedicated/Hosted, you pick a region and we keep your traffic in-region; cross-region failover is optional and would be something you opt into.

[10:12] Marcus Reed: So if you’re saying “optional,” I want to be clear: is there any automatic failover that would push data to another region if the region is down?

[10:20] Markus Klein: Not without explicit configuration. Default is same-region only. If you want multi-region, we’d set it up intentionally and document it.

[10:30] Fatima Noor: And we can put it in the architecture diagram and the contract exhibit. So there’s no ambiguity for auditors.

[10:38] Tom Kline: That’s helpful.

[10:40] Jen Alvarez: What happens if the region is down then? Like do we just get errors.

[10:44] Markus Klein: In single-region, yes—your service is down with that region. Some customers prefer that because it’s compliant. Others do warm standby in another region but still keep data controls. But that’s your policy decision.

[10:58] Nina Patel: For us it’s not just compliance, it’s also “we don’t want unknown data copies.” So single-region is fine for pilot.

[11:07] Markus Klein: Got it.

[11:09] Avery Johnson: Marcus, you also asked about KMS/HSM.

[11:12] Marcus Reed: Yeah. We use AWS KMS with customer-managed keys. In some cases we have CloudHSM, but KMS is baseline.

[11:20] Fatima Noor: For Private, encryption at rest is using your storage services—EBS/EFS/S3—so it’s your KMS keys by default. For app-level secrets, we integrate with your secrets manager patterns. For in-transit, it’s TLS.

[11:35] Marcus Reed: Any part of the runtime that uses its own keys?

[11:38] Fatima Noor: Not in Private. In Hosted/Dedicated we manage encryption keys, with options for customer-managed keys depending on tier. But if your requirement is “all keys are ours,” Private is the cleanest.

[11:53] Nina Patel: And control plane—does it need to phone home? That’s the thing.

[11:57] Markus Klein: There are two variants. One is “connected Private,” where the control plane can reach Redwood for updates and telemetry. The other is more isolated, where we minimize or remove external connectivity and you manage upgrades via packages. The second is more common for on-prem or stricter regulated customers.

[12:17] Marcus Reed: We can allow outbound to a fixed endpoint, but we prefer not. We can discuss.

[12:22] Avery Johnson: That’s exactly what the security review is for.

[12:25] Markus Klein: Let me show routing in a Private-ish context. The routing policy engine is the same—you define primary and fallback. In Private, the fallbacks are typically other deployments in the same cluster.

[12:40] Jen Alvarez: For fraud ops, latency matters but not like chat-level. We do batch too.

[12:45] Markus Klein: Great. Batch workloads often benefit from continuous batching and larger batch sizes. In Dedicated/Private we can tune those.

[12:55] Nina Patel: What about throughput predictability? That’s why we looked at Dedicated.

[13:00] Markus Klein: In Private, predictability is determined by what GPU you allocate and your autoscaling config. Dedicated gives you “we guarantee a pool.” Private gives you “you guarantee a pool” because it’s yours.

[13:14] Avery Johnson: But we still provide recommended sizing and we can do a benchmark with your sequence length distribution.

[13:20] Nina Patel: Okay.

[13:22] Markus Klein: Back to Console: rollouts. If you want to test a new quantization profile or a new model version, you can do a canary at 5% traffic, monitor latency and error rate, then ramp.

[13:36] Jen Alvarez: If we do a smaller model for fallback, can we restrict it to certain customers? Like, premium gets big model.

[13:44] Markus Klein: Yes, you can route by request attributes. Like account tier, route, or region. You can also use headers for that. We’d define it in policy.

[13:57] Marcus Reed: Headers can be spoofed though.

[13:59] Markus Klein: Right, you’d do it behind your gateway or sign it. We can talk about best practices.

[14:06] Fatima Noor: Typically the customer’s API gateway enforces the identity, then Redwood sees a trusted claim.

[14:14] Nina Patel: That makes sense.

[14:16] Avery Johnson: Markus, can you show what happens during an incident? Like what you see.

[14:20] Markus Klein: Yep. There’s an Errors view. It groups errors by type: timeouts, rate limits, upstream issues. In Private, you get runtime-level metrics, plus we can integrate with your PagerDuty.

[14:35] Jen Alvarez: Do you do automated rollback?

[14:37] Markus Klein: You can configure automatic fallback/rollback if a canary degrades. Like, if P95 latency > X for 5 minutes, revert. But again, you define it.

[14:50] Nina Patel: Okay.

[14:51] Marcus Reed: Back to audit logs—does it include reads? Like when someone views a prompt or views traces.

[14:58] Fatima Noor: In the Console, yes we can log access events for admin-level actions and certain views, but it depends on what UI features are enabled. For Private, if the UI is in your environment, you can log those events locally. We should confirm your exact requirement: is it “all admin actions,” or also “every read of metadata.”

[15:22] Marcus Reed: For us it’s admin actions at minimum. Reads would be nice.

[15:27] Fatima Noor: Great, we’ll capture that.

[15:30] Tom Kline: Also, do you support SSO? Sorry, tangential.

[15:33] Fatima Noor: Yes—SSO/SAML, plus RBAC. SCIM depends on setup. We can go deeper in security review.

[15:42] Marcus Reed: SCIM is one of the checkboxes.

[15:44] Avery Johnson: We’ve had a few SCIM edge cases but generally yes. We’ll validate for your IdP.

[15:50] Markus Klein: I’ll pause and ask: what are the top two workloads you’re thinking for the pilot, just so we keep the demo relevant.

[15:57] Jen Alvarez: For fraud ops: summarizing case notes, and maybe generating a next-best-action suggestion for analysts. Second is customer support—agent assist. We want to reduce handle time.

[16:12] Nina Patel: And from platform side, we want it to live in our VPC. We can give you a staging account.

[16:19] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[16:21] Avery Johnson: And just to confirm, you mentioned latency targets previously. Was it like 1-2 seconds for support?

[16:27] Jen Alvarez: Yeah, like under two seconds for the first token would be good. But fraud is more like, under 10 seconds is okay if it’s accurate.

[16:36] Markus Klein: That’s helpful.

[16:38] Marcus Reed: And compliance: no data outside us-east. Prefer no cross-region. Logs to Splunk. Encryption with our KMS.

[16:48] Fatima Noor: Noted.

[16:50] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick Q&A section now.

[16:53] Avery Johnson: Yeah, go for it.

[16:55] Marcus Reed: In Private, who has access to the cluster? Do Redwood engineers get access.

[17:02] Fatima Noor: By default, no standing access. Support access is customer-controlled, time-bound, and auditable. Many customers require a break-glass process. We can support that. If you want fully air-gapped support, that’s also possible, just slower.

[17:21] Marcus Reed: Okay. And do you have SOC 2.

[17:24] Avery Johnson: Yes, we can share the report under NDA via the evidence pack process.

[17:28] Tom Kline: We’ll need that for procurement.

[17:30] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[17:32] Nina Patel: For Private, what’s the upgrade process? Like do we have to take downtime.

[17:38] Markus Klein: We support rolling upgrades. You can run two versions side-by-side and shift traffic. But the exact mechanics depend on your orchestrator—Kubernetes usually.

[17:50] Nina Patel: We are on EKS, yes.

[17:52] Markus Klein: Great.

[17:54] Jen Alvarez: Model options—are we limited to certain models?

[17:58] Markus Klein: We have a catalog of supported models. In Private, we can work with you to onboard if needed, but we typically start with a known stable set. We can also advise on quantization profiles.

[18:11] Jen Alvarez: We’ve tried OpenAI and Bedrock. Bedrock was… expensive.

[18:15] Avery Johnson: Yeah, we hear that. We can talk unit economics in follow-up.

[18:20] Marcus Reed: Another security question: do you do any training on our data.

[18:24] Avery Johnson: No training on customer data. In Private, it’s your environment anyway.

[18:29] Fatima Noor: And in Hosted/Dedicated, we have contractual commitments. We can cover in security review.

[18:35] Marcus Reed: Okay.

[18:37] Nina Patel: Fallback question. If the big model is unavailable, will it silently go to the small one. Because that could change outputs and cause issues.

[18:45] Markus Klein: It only does what you configure. If you don’t want fallback, we turn it off. Or you can require an explicit header like “allow_fallback=true” for certain routes.

[18:57] Nina Patel: That’s good.

[19:00] Jen Alvarez: For my team, I’d rather it fail with a clear error than hallucinate on a tiny model.

[19:06] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Some people do “fallback to a safe template response” instead. Like return “We’re experiencing delays, please try again.”

[19:14] Jen Alvarez: Yeah.

[19:15] Avery Johnson: Anything else from procurement side, Tom?

[19:18] Tom Kline: Just: can we buy through AWS Marketplace? That’s easier.

[19:23] Avery Johnson: We can. For Private it depends on structure but yes, we do private offers. We can bring partnerships in.

[19:31] Tom Kline: Great.

[19:33] Marcus Reed: Back to audit logs one more time. Can you show an example event?

[19:38] Markus Klein: I don’t have your Private environment obviously, but I can show a sample from our docs. (pause) Basically looks like: event_type=policy.update, actor=user_id, timestamp, resource_id, diff hash.

[19:55] Marcus Reed: Diff hash?

[19:57] Markus Klein: Like a reference to the config change. Sometimes people log the old/new config. In regulated setups, they often log a pointer to the change record and store the actual config in Git.

[20:10] Nina Patel: We do GitOps. That would be fine.

[20:13] Fatima Noor: If you do GitOps, you get a lot of auditability for free. Redwood audit logs cover the control plane actions; your Git history covers desired state.

[20:23] Marcus Reed: Ok.

[20:25] Avery Johnson: We’re at 20 minutes but it feels like we covered the big questions. Markus, anything else you want to show?

[20:31] Markus Klein: Maybe just quick: region pinning. In Console, deployments have a region label. Policies can require region match. In Private it’s inherent. In Dedicated, you can specify “only run in region X.”

[20:45] Marcus Reed: And no data leaves region.

[20:47] Markus Klein: Correct.

[20:49] Avery Johnson: Cool. Let’s talk about a pilot plan for 5 minutes.

[20:53] Nina Patel: Yes please.

[20:55] Avery Johnson: What we’ve seen work: pick one route, like fraud case summary. Define success metrics: latency P95 under 10 sec, cost under some threshold per case, and quality measured on a small eval set. Then run in your VPC in a staging account.

[21:13] Jen Alvarez: I can provide like 200 redacted cases.

[21:16] Marcus Reed: Redaction is tricky.

[21:18] Jen Alvarez: We can strip names, maybe.

[21:20] Fatima Noor: For the pilot, we can also do “synthetic” or “PHI-free” dataset to validate architecture first, then you decide whether to run real data later.

[21:32] Nina Patel: That might be easiest.

[21:34] Avery Johnson: Great. Then in parallel we do security review and evidence pack. Once security is comfortable, we can expand dataset.

[21:45] Tom Kline: Timeline: if we like it, procurement is like… 6 to 8 weeks.

[21:50] Avery Johnson: That’s consistent. We can try to keep technical validation to 2-3 weeks so it doesn’t drag.

[21:58] Marcus Reed: For security review, we will need SOC2, encryption diagram, retention statement, and audit log sample.

[22:06] Fatima Noor: Noted. We have an evidence pack index and we can share under NDA.

[22:12] Avery Johnson: We’ll coordinate that.

[22:14] Nina Patel: One more: does Private mean on-prem is also possible? We’re not now, but long term maybe.

[22:20] Markus Klein: Yes, there’s an on-prem package. Same concepts, just different installer. But we’ll focus on VPC first.

[22:28] Nina Patel: Okay.

[22:30] Avery Johnson: Let’s do recap and next steps.

[22:33] Avery Johnson: From Redwood side: I’ll send a recap with (1) deployment options and recommended architecture for your VPC constraint, (2) proposed pilot plan and success criteria template, and (3) scheduling links for security review.

[22:47] Fatima Noor: I’ll follow up with audit log schema details and how export works—JSON, forwarding to Splunk, and what’s configurable around retention.

[22:57] Markus Klein: And if you want, we can run a quick benchmark sizing exercise once you tell us expected concurrency and prompt sizes.

[23:05] Nina Patel: We can share estimates.

[23:07] Marcus Reed: I’ll send the questionnaire. And I’ll want to confirm the “no cross region” default in writing.

[23:13] Avery Johnson: Yep, we’ll put it in the email.

[23:15] Tom Kline: And I’ll check AWS Marketplace path on our side.

[23:19] Jen Alvarez: I’ll define which workflow to pilot first. Probably fraud summary.

[23:25] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Any last questions?

[23:29] (crosstalk)

[23:31] Marcus Reed: None.

[23:32] Nina Patel: Good.

[23:34] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

[23:36] (Meeting ends)

Note: Transcript ends early in Fireflies export; remaining time in calendar invite included screen-share wrap-up and internal notes. Key decisions and next steps captured above.
